opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about this a lot, and honestly I don't see the two as being in tension as much as people assume.

The way I frame it is that mathematics is the cleanest possible testbed for reasoning. When you work in a formal language like Lean, every step can be checked. There's no ambiguity about whether the model got it right. So if you can build systems that genuinely discover and verify new mathematics, you've built something whose core capability, reliable, verifiable reasoning, is valuable far beyond math. That's the bet.

On the ambition side, we want to push toward something like an AI mathematician: a system that can propose conjectures, construct proofs, and formalize them, all in a loop where the verifier keeps it honest. That's a long-horizon research goal, and we're not shy about it.

But you can't just sit in a room for ten years waiting for a breakthrough. So the business question becomes: where does verifiable reasoning create value today? There's a natural bridge to formal verification of software and hardware. Chip design, safety-critical code, cryptographic protocols, financial systems. These are places where "probably correct" isn't good enough and people already pay a lot for correctness. The same machinery that proves a theorem can prove that a piece of code does what it's supposed to do.

There's also the data flywheel. Every proof the system finds and verifies becomes high-quality training data with a guaranteed-correct label, which is scarce in most domains. That compounds over time and becomes a real moat.

So the discipline for us as a team is sequencing. Keep the north star very ambitious, but make sure each milestone along the way is something that's useful on its own, to mathematicians, to engineers, to customers. If every intermediate step has standalone value, the research and the business reinforce each other rather than compete for oxygen.

And personally, coming from a math background, I care that mathematicians see this as a tool that amplifies them. If we earn that trust in the community, I think that's also what makes the company durable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses sequencing milestones and earning mathematicians’ trust, but does not frame building a lasting company as a responsibility to employees or the founding team.

r002.rationale: It presents becoming an AI mathematician as a long-horizon research goal and says the team should keep an ambitious north star, making moonshot ambition central to its direction.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think of them as being in tension, honestly. If anything, the "AI for Math" ambition is the reason the business can exist, and the business is the thing that keeps the ambition honest.

Let me explain what I mean by that. The long-term goal is a system that can genuinely do mathematics, not just pattern-match on competition problems, but formalize, verify, and eventually discover things that humans haven't. That's a decades-long project. You can't fund it with grant money, and you can't fund it purely on investor enthusiasm either, because enthusiasm has a half-life. So you need revenue, and you need it from people who actually have a problem that mathematical reasoning solves today.

The nice thing is that those problems are real. If you look at where formal verification matters, chip design, cryptography, safety-critical software, finance, people are already paying for correctness, they're just paying for it in a very expensive, very manual way. Lean, Coq, Isabelle, all of these have existed for a long time, but the bottleneck has always been that writing proofs is slow and requires specialists. If you can make an AI system that closes that gap, even partially, that's a product customers will pay for right now, not in ten years.

So the way I think about it is: every commercial problem we take on should be a stepping stone toward the research goal, and every research result should be something we can eventually put into the product. If a contract would pull us toward building something that has nothing to do with reasoning, we don't take it. And if a research direction is beautiful but can never touch reality, we're probably not the right place for it, that's what universities are for.

The other piece is discipline about the team. It's tempting to hire fifty people the moment you raise money. We've tried to stay small and dense, people who are genuinely strong in mathematics and in machine learning, because a small team that ships things is far better than a large team arguing about roadmaps. That also keeps burn low, which means we have a long runway to be wrong a few times, and we will be wrong a few times.

So I'd put it this way: the ambition sets the direction, the business sets the pace. If you only have the ambition, you run out of money before you get there. If you only have the business, you end up building a consulting shop and you never get there at all. You need both, and you need to be honest with yourself every quarter about whether you're still actually on the path.

r001.rationale: The response discusses revenue, runway, and keeping the team small, but does not frame building a lasting company as a founder’s responsibility to employees or the early founding team.

r002.rationale: It presents the “AI for Math” ambition as the reason the business exists and says the ambition sets the company’s direction.

astra-6.text:
I think the ambition and the business have to reinforce each other. AI for math is a long-term research challenge, so you need a business that gives you the resources and patience to keep working on it. At the same time, you need to build something useful along the way—something people value enough to pay for.

The balance is in choosing those near-term problems carefully. Does solving this customer’s problem also help us build toward deeper mathematical reasoning? If it does, then revenue and research progress can support each other. If it pulls us in a completely different direction, even an attractive opportunity can become a distraction.

So I’d want us to be ambitious about the destination and disciplined about the next step. A lasting business needs to deliver value today while continuing to earn the right to pursue that bigger vision.

r001.rationale: The response discusses building a lasting business but does not frame it as a responsibility to employees or the founding team.

r002.rationale: It describes AI for math as a long-term challenge and refers to a bigger vision, but does not clearly state that moonshot ambition is fundamental to the company’s identity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the ambition and the business have to reinforce each other. If we want to make meaningful progress on AI for math, we need the resources and the team to work on hard problems over a long period of time. That makes building a lasting business part of the mission.

The balance is in choosing what to build along the way. What can we deliver today that solves a real problem for someone, and also moves us toward the capabilities we ultimately want? Revenue gives us sustainability, but customers also give us feedback about whether those capabilities are actually useful.

There’s a tension, of course. The most interesting research question isn’t always the most urgent customer need. I think you have to be deliberate about making room for both, and honest about what each project is supposed to accomplish.

r001.rationale: The response says a lasting business provides resources and a team for long-term work, but does not frame it as the founder’s responsibility to employees or the early founding team.

r002.rationale: It describes meaningful progress on AI for math as part of the mission, but does not identify moonshot ambition as fundamental to the company’s identity.
